title: Palindrome Partitioning III
statement:
You get a string `s` of lowercase English letters and an integer `k`. First you may overwrite any of the characters of `s` with other lowercase letters. After that, `s` must be cut into exactly `k` non-empty contiguous pieces that cover the whole string, and every piece must be a palindrome (it reads the same forwards and backwards).

Return the smallest number of characters you have to overwrite to make such a cut possible.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Once the pieces are fixed, each one is repaired on its own: a piece becomes a palindrome after changing one character of every mirrored pair that differs. So the problem splits into two parts. First, precompute that repair cost for every substring. Second, choose where to cut so that the sum of the `k` repair costs is smallest. Trying every set of cut positions is exponential, but the best way to split a prefix into `c` pieces only depends on the prefix length and `c`, so dynamic programming handles it.

## Approach

1. Build `cost[left][right]`, the changes needed to make `s[left..right]` a palindrome, by growing substrings by length: it is the inner substring's cost plus 1 when the two outer letters differ.
2. Let `dp[parts][end]` be the fewest changes to split the first `end` characters into `parts` palindromes; `dp[0][0] = 0` and everything else starts at `Infinity`.
3. For each `parts` and `end`, try every `start` of the last piece: `dp[parts - 1][start] + cost[start][end - 1]`, and keep the minimum.
4. Return `dp[k][n]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "abc"`, `k = 2`. Single letters cost 0; `cost[0][1] = 1` (`a` vs `b`), `cost[1][2] = 1`, and `cost[0][2] = cost[1][1] + 1 = 1` (`a` vs `c`).
With one piece, `dp[1][1] = 0`, `dp[1][2] = 1`, `dp[1][3] = 1`.
For two pieces of the whole string, `dp[2][3]` tries `start = 1` ("a" + "bc": 0 + 1) and `start = 2` ("ab" + "c": 1 + 0), so the answer is `1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(k · n²): the cost table is O(n²) and each of the k · n states tries up to n starts.
- Space: O(n² + k · n) for the two tables.

## Pitfalls

- Recomputing a substring's repair cost inside the split loop adds another factor of n; precompute `cost` once.
- Every piece must be non-empty, so `start` begins at `parts - 1` (each earlier piece needs at least one letter).
- Fill `cost` by increasing length, so the inner substring is ready when you need it.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `s` |
| `cost[left][right]` | changes needed to make `s[left..right]` a palindrome |
| `length`, `left`, `right` | the substring being costed |
| `dp[parts][end]` | fewest changes to split the first `end` letters into `parts` palindromes |
| `start` | where the last piece begins |
| `candidate` | total changes when the last piece is `s[start..end-1]` |
